434. Having covered them thickly with fat: with the caul, in which they wrap the sacrificial victims so that they may burn very well.
436. Gazing at: Homer uses 'to gaze at' for 'to marvel at' (κ 180): 'they gazed at the deer'; but Apollonius uses it for 'to look at'. L

438. With purple coils: with the smoke's convolutions turning purple, with the fire's twists and [as it were purpling] spirals; the expression is vivid.
441. Bringing the fleece: he should have said 'bringing' in agreement with 'you' (v. 440). And the poet too (A 541): 'always it is dear to you to be apart from me'. L
444. Of Asia: Asia was named after Asia, the mother of Prometheus and daughter of Atlas; but others say from having much mud (ἄσις). L

445-47a. Thus with evil 〈bonds〉: not from the general, but from the things harmful to me. It is a hyperbaton and the conjunction 'and' is redundant, the preposition 'from' is missing, and the case is changed, dative instead of genitive. The verb is also in the perfect tense, instead of 'I went out'. The sense is this: having known beforehand from evil omens my own fate, I went out from my homeland, so that by sailing with you I might win renown. L
b. So that I might embark: it is a hyperbaton. The order is: so that I might embark on the ship, and for the one who has embarked on the ship, good repute might be left to his household. L
450. Steadfast: instead of 'scorching' and 'hot'; he speaks of midday from what happens, since the sun, having culminated, warms
all things because it is equally distant from the things below on all sides, or because it stands still, for the sun seems to move less then.
454. Of the gray: because it is whitened by being washed by the waves. And 'leafage' means the bed of leaves.
456a. Sweet: derived from 'exceedingly fitted' or from λῶ, 'I wish'. Hesiod says (fr. 207 Rz.²) 'with sweet feet': those pleasing to the sight.
